episode.episode: Philips Hue: The smart home’s light bulb moment
episode.showDescription: Version History is a show about the best gadgets ever. And the worst ones. And the ones that might have changed the world, if they ever actually shipped. Every week, your favorite people from The Verge and beyond hang out to tell and debate the story of a gadget, app, website, or any other tech product, and try to determine the item’s true legacy. Because not every product is a hit, but every product has a story. And the ones that really matter aren’t always the ones you think. From the Verge and the Vox Media Podcast Network.
episode.episodeDescription: The humble light bulb might be the ultimate success story in the smart home. Our connected, adaptable homes are supposed to be customizable, connected to everything, and incredibly easy to use, and nothing has made that work quite like Philips Hue lights. In this episode, The Verge's David Pierce and Jennifer Pattison Tuohy are joined by smart home journalist and expert Richard Gunther to tell the Hue's story. We trace the product's history from its origins in the smartphone revolution, try to figure out how Philips managed to turn a staggeringly expensive lightbulb into a must-have gadget, and look at whether there's even more invention left in the future of lighting. Yeah, it was actually kind of wild coming into the studio and seeing how much these don't look like light bulbs.

There was a wired story when these first ones came out that called them smushed ice cream tons, which I think is exactly the mental image that everyone should have in their mind if you're listening to this.
So we should take a break here because this is a good moment, but we're going to leave the story at CES 2012.
A bunch of stuff has happened.
It's one of those things where there's a lot of tech to build and there's a lot going on, but everyone pretty quickly understood the power of this thing.
It wasn't like he had to go and fight for his belief.
It was like, no, they put this in front of people and everybody immediately was like, oh my gosh, this is amazing.
But what they have to figure out how to do now is sell the most expensive light bulbs you can possibly imagine to people.
